meta.title: Who really said "You Cannot Persuade Her with Gun or Lariat, To Come Across for the Proletariat"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Dorothy Parker did, and there is a first-hand witness: Somerset Maugham printed the lines in 1944, describing watching her write them. The party anecdote is the wrong part.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You Cannot Persuade Her with Gun or Lariat, To Come Across for the Proletariat'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Parker’s, documented by Maugham in 1944. What is wrong is the story around it — she was not challenged to finish a nursery rhyme.

answer.label: Written by Dorothy Parker
answer.authorDates: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic and short-story writer
answer.sourceLine: These lines are genuinely Parker’s, and the witness is about as good as quotation research gets: W. Somerset Maugham ↗ printed them in his introduction to The Viking Portable Library: Dorothy Parker (1944), describing a Hollywood dinner party at which he asked Parker to write him a poem and watched her do it. Quote Investigator ↗ verified that source on paper and concludes: “Dorothy Parker crafted this clever poem.” What is wrong is not the attribution but the anecdote that travels with it.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: W. Somerset Maugham, introduction to The Viking Portable Library: Dorothy Parker, pp. 12–14
A Hollywood dinner party at Fanny Brice’s; Maugham asked Parker for a poem

source.excerpt:
Higgledy Piggledy, my white hen;
She lays eggs for gentlemen.

“Yes, I’ve always liked those lines,” I said.
She gave a thin, cool smile and without an instant’s hesitation, added:

You cannot persuade her with gun or lariat
To come across for the proletariat.
trail: Quote Investigator’s article ↗ is the anchor. It traces the story to Maugham’s introduction to the 1944 Viking Portable Library: Dorothy Parker, quotes his account at length, and concludes that Parker did write the poem.

Maugham’s account is first-hand and specific. He describes the party (at Fanny Brice’s, with Aldous Huxley among the guests), his request for a poem, the waiter sent for a pencil and “gone a long time,” and Parker writing out the nursery-rhyme couplet before adding her own. That level of circumstantial detail from a named eyewitness is unusually strong for a Round Table-era quip.

The couplet is stable across the record. QI notes that John Keats’s 1970 Parker biography You Might as Well Live “hewed closely to the version given by Maugham in 1944,” and Bartlett’s Book of Anecdotes reproduces the same two lines in 2000.

The 1944 volume itself is held by the Internet Archive ↗ — The Viking Press, 1944, with Parker as the credited author. The item is lending-restricted, so we could not open the introduction and read Maugham’s pages ourselves; we confirmed that the edition exists and is the one QI cites, and we rely on QI’s reading of the text.
source.excerptNote: That is Quote Investigator’s transcription ↗ of Maugham’s 1944 introduction, which frames the verse with his own narration. The first two lines are a traditional nursery rhyme that Parker wrote out; the second two are hers. This page’s headline uses the title-case, single-line form the couplet usually circulates in — the source sets it as two lines of verse.

source.rightsNote: The verse was first published in 1944, well after the 1930 cut-off below which US works are reliably in the public domain, so it is treated here as in copyright. Parker left her estate to Martin Luther King Jr. and, on his death, to the NAACP ↗, which is therefore the party to approach about her literary rights; the 1944 volume was published by The Viking Press. The two lines are quoted here for commentary on their attribution. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Dorothy Parker
author.heading: About Dorothy Parker
author.metaLine: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic and short-story writer
author.bio: Dorothy Parker (born Dorothy Rothschild, 22 August 1893 – 7 June 1967) was an American poet, critic and short-story writer, a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table, and by the 1930s a working Hollywood screenwriter — which is how she came to be at a Los Angeles dinner party with Maugham and Aldous Huxley. Light verse was her first trade and her most disciplined one, and this couplet shows the technique: a comic rhyme carrying a political joke, delivered without visible effort.

misattribution.heading: The story around it is the wrong part
misattribution.intro: The verse is Parker’s and well sourced. The anecdote it usually arrives in has been reshaped into a better story than the one Maugham actually told.

items.who: A party game of completing nursery rhymes
items.why: The familiar telling — guests challenging each other to finish rhymes, Maugham handing Parker a couplet to cap — appears in Bartlett’s Book of Anecdotes (2000). In Maugham’s own 1944 account ↗ there was no game and no challenge: he asked her to write him a poem, and she wrote all four lines herself.

QI notes that Parker had a long wait while the waiter fetched a pencil, and “may have thought about or constructed the poem before she even attended the party.” Maugham says only that she added the couplet “without an instant’s hesitation” once he spoke.

items.who: “my fine hen … But she won’t, by gun or lariat”
items.why: QI records an altered version in a Michigan newspaper editorial in 1971, still credited to Parker. The 1944 text reads “my white hen” and “You cannot persuade her with gun or lariat.”

misattribution.truthLine: Parker wrote it, Maugham printed it in 1944, and the only thing that needed correcting was the story — see Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke is a collision of registers. “Higgledy Piggledy, my white hen” is a nursery rhyme; “come across for the proletariat” is 1930s left-wing political vocabulary, with “come across” carrying its period slang sense of giving something up under pressure. Parker sets a hen against the class struggle and lets the rhyme do the rest.

The politics were not decorative. Parker was seriously engaged with left-wing causes in the 1930s and 1940s, which is what makes the couplet a joke at her own expense as much as anyone else’s — the hen is the one holdout no amount of organising can recruit.
detailsBody: This page is filed as verified, which on this site means a specific published work has been shown to contain the wording. That work is Maugham’s 1944 introduction, and the reader should know exactly how far our own checking went: we confirmed the 1944 Viking Press edition exists and is the one cited, but the Internet Archive copy is lending-restricted and we could not read the introduction inside it. Quote Investigator reports verifying it on paper, and we cite QI as the reader.

It is a useful case for what “misattributed” can mean. Nothing about the credit is wrong here. What had drifted was the narrative — and a good anecdote will reshape itself toward a better story just as reliably as an orphaned quip will drift toward a more famous name.
context.pull: Parker sets a hen against the class struggle and lets the rhyme do the rest.
